chapter: Growing up: theaters and the lakefront
title: Liberty Theater usher job, the Sanger Theater drum job and Lou Forbes
summary: Hirsch worked as an usher at the Liberty, learned its theater musicians, then took over the drum chair at the Sanger when Gosley quit and learned stage presence from Lou Forbes.

story.theme_name: Medicine shows, minstrels, circuses and the black theater circuit
story.community_name: On the road with minstrel, carnival and tent shows

blocks.x: No, they were all readers. They played overtures and things like that. Overtures and played, that's how I got to know all this crap. I mean, in fact, when I went to this, when I was in high school, I got a job at the Liberty Theater as an usher working just weekends in high school during the school season. I think we got a dollar or two dollars a day. And you'd always get tips on Saturday and Sunday when you'd have an over crowd of people and you'd get people to sit. You have one of these flash boxes with green lights and red lights. I mean, two seats to one seat and you're down there front. You come down when you get them a seat. After standing there for ten minutes, they give you a nickel or a dime. And I took the job because I could get my wife and I could get my mother and my sister into the show for nothing to see the pictures. And then I used to go over to Glucks right across the street and eat dinner for 25 cents in those days. And in the winter and the summertime, then I worked steady. That's where I got to know Ray McNamara and Bob Martin on the organ. Because I used to stay in there late to put a cage over the, you had to have like a cage and put it over the petals. So they had rats in the theater and the rats used to eat the felt out of the petals. They would do that and ruin the petals. They had to put a cage on top of it. They had to put a cage like on top of the, on top of the petals. So that the rats wouldn't get to them. And that's how I got to know Bob Martin and Ray McNamara. When they were down there at different times. And then they had a pianist by the name of Vital Lubowski. Vit Lubowski, Tony Perranti, Tony Popalia, Jimmy, Jimmy, Boyle, the drummer. Johnny Karooge on fiddle. And Henry Connect I think was playing trumpet. And I think Tug Popalia was playing trombone. I'm not sure. And that's how I got to know these guys. And when I went to the Sanger Theater, I went in there as a substitute. And Gosley came back and he was all excited about, they were telling me how well it is. Well you like the guys so well. You like the kids so well. Well god damn it, go ahead and get them. I quit. So Fontana rings me up. Oddly enough I'd use Gosley's drums instead of moving my stuff down there. And he rings me up at 8 o'clock in the morning when I thought Gosley was going to be back for rehearsal. And he said, kid, come on down for rehearsal. I said, what's the matter, Gosley didn't get in? He said, yes he's in but he's quitting. I said, what's the matter? He said, I don't know. He said, but he quit. And he says, if you don't want the job I'm going to get another drummer. I told him, I said, I don't want the job. He said, well if you don't want it, I'm going to get somebody else. So I went down there and that's when I got the job at the Sanger Theater. But it was, and then I was there for a couple of weeks and then I wanted to go to California with the Tulane band. So I put Gosley in for two weeks and by the time he got finished in two weeks he lost it up so great that they didn't even want him back. So that was when Lou Forbes was there. And then that's when Lou Forbes took hold of me and started teaching me to stand up when I play. When you make a mistake, smile. If you make a mistake, you've got to play the same thing over again, make the same mistake. That's right.
That's a trick. They don't know that you made a mistake.
And Forbes was an educator. He taught Lou Primer how to bow, how to take a bow.
That is interesting. So what we were talking about before. What's that? How you got to know Primer and how you...
